quote: Automating the task involves addressing three main subtasks: translation of the spoken content, segmentation of the translated text into blocks and lines, and estimation of the timestamps for each block.
We introduce the first fully end-to-end AS solution that seamlessly produces both subtitles (i.e., segmented translations) and their timestamps without any reliance on intermediate transcripts.
Subtitling aims to facilitate the accessibility of audiovisual media, such as movies, TV shows, and video lectures, by providing users with a textual translation of spoken content.
models: Direct autoregressive encoder-decoder model with Conformer encoder and Transformer decoder
outputs: Generated subtitles (segmented translations) with start and end timestamps

We evaluate our solutions automatically through comparative experiments ... using SubER (↓) and SubSONAR (↑) as the main metrics, complemented by AS‑BLEU/BLEU, CPS and CPL conformity scores.
We introduce SubSONAR, a novel metric for evaluating timestamp quality ( §4), which is based on SONAR and designed to be sensitive to time shifts, enabling a focused evaluation of timestamps.
The evaluation was carried out by two annotators per language pair, who are proficient in English (C1) as well as native speakers or very proficient (C2) in the target language (German or Spanish).

We conducted the first-ever manual evaluation of timestamp quality in subtitling. The evaluation was carried out by two annotators per language pair, who are proficient in English and native speakers of the target language. We instructed the annotators with ad‑hoc guidelines to adjust the start, end, or both timestamps when the generated subtitles are not synchronized with the speech.

To corroborate the findings from our automatic evaluation, we conducted the first-ever manual evaluation of timestamp quality in subtitling. This evaluation was specifically conducted on the two language pairs addressed in our high-resource experiments (en-de, en-es).
guideline: You are asked to check if the source language speech and its corresponding translated subtitles are synchronized, that is if the subtitle remains on screen for the right amount of time with respect to the corresponding speech. If the timing is wrong, move the timestamp of each subtitle such that the timing of the subtitle matches the timing of the audio.
Annotators were asked to adjust the start, end, or both timestamps to achieve synchronization between subtitle text and audio, following detailed annotation guidelines.
